newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania plans new insurance law to boost reforms.
newsitem.headline: Romania plans new insurance law to boost reforms.

text.p: Romania will issue a new insurance bill this year to foster free-market reforms and to attract foreign investors, Finance Minister Mircea Ciumara said on Wednesday.
"We badly need foreign investments and a developed local insurance bussiness is one of the things investors are looking for," Ciumara told a one-day conference on the domestic insurance sector.
Since the 1989 fall of communism, Romania, which drew only $2.3 billion in direct foreign investments, has been slow in dismantling the state monopoly of insurance.
Despite a mushrooming of private insurers, the market is thin with their turnover only accounting for 0.4 percent of gross domestic product.

"The new bill will be aligned to Western standards, offering greater cover for insurance policy holders," said Varujan Vosganian, head of the finance and budget commision on parliament's upper Senate.

Minimum equity requirements have been unchanged since 1991. Existing rules allow anyone having around $4,000 in his pocket to set up an insurance firm in Romania, where the total capital of insurers stands at only 127 billion lei ($18 million).
The new project pledges to increase minimum capital requirements, strengthen the powers of local supervisors and put severe sanctions for breaching rules.
Most of the 53 insurers operating in Romania are dwarfed by the state-owned ASIROM, which controls half of the market and had the monopoly of compulsory insurance until last year.

A few big international names have come to the Romanian market, with Italy's Assicurazioni Generali Spa and American International Group Inc operating joint ventures and ING Group ready to enter the life insurance field soon.
"We expect the new (insurance) bill to pass in parliament's next session, after summer recess" said Vosganian, a member of the ruling centrist coalition which dominates parliament.

Last year Romania scrapped communist-era mandatory insurance cover for property and vehicle passengers. But it has built little by way of a commercial safety nets for individuals and companies, with theft, pensions, crops and health insurance almost unavailable.
